Project Summary¶

This project focused on developing an intelligent medical chatbot designed to assist doctors by summarizing patient complaints and medical histories. The motivation behind the project is to address the challenge of handling large volumes of patient data efficiently, reducing the time doctors spend manually reviewing patient notes, and improving the overall patient experience.

We implemented a Natural Language Processing pipeline using the T5 model to generate concise summaries of patient problems based on raw input text. The project involved fine-tuning the T5 transformer model on a medical dataset consisting of patient descriptions, complaints, and diagnostic notes. We worked with 250,000 patient descriptions so that the model could understand what patients want when they are sick. The chatbot takes in a patient's problem description, processes it, and returns a summary. Based on that summary, the model calls an API through Streamlit apps to help the patient understand what needs to be done.

This project not only gives patients suggestions but also stores their past information. In our body, one problem is often related to other problems. So, based on the patient's previous issues, the chatbot provides feedback. It not only helps the patient but also assists doctors by informing them of the patient's previous conditions. This comprehensive approach enhances the quality of care and enables more informed decision-making. The dataset we downloaded from Hugging Face and all the preprocessing we have done are saved in the below google drive link. If anyone is interested in working with this preprocessed data, they can simply download it from here.

Google drive link - https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1v6KRSdGiOeqN2Slg9CyqTZWFc07XPNR2?usp=share_link git_experiment_link - https://github.com/Md-SadmanSakib/medical_chatbot.git

2.Loading The Dataset¶

The dataset contains description, patient, and doctor fields, where "patient" represents the patient's problem and "description" is a concise summary of that problem. The "doctor" field contains the doctor's suggestion. We aim to create a chatbot that will utilize the concise summaries we have generated by training on the patient data. In this system, the role of the doctor will be played by an API, allowing us to provide up-to-date medical advice based on the generated summaries.

This approach combines the power of our trained model for understanding and summarizing patient issues with the flexibility of an external API for medical recommendations. By doing so, we can create a more dynamic and potentially more accurate medical chatbot that can adapt to new medical information as it becomes available through the API.

3.Text Pre-processing¶

3.1 Text Cleaning¶

When working with a text dataset, the most important part is cleaning. The better the cleaning, the more effectively the model will be able to capture the text. In this text preprocessing step, I have gone through several text cleaning processes to get better outcomes from the patient features and the description features. Our approach is creating a better and more concise summarization, so we did not perform all hard cleaning of the dataset because we need to capture the meaning

3.1a First stage of text cleaning¶

In [38]:
import re
import pandas as pd
import spacy
from multiprocessing import cpu_count
import contractions

# Initialize SpaCy with only necessary components
nlp = spacy.load("en_core_web_sm", disable=["parser", "ner", "textcat"])

# Define custom stopwords 
custom_stopwords = set([
    "the", "a", "an", "and", "or", "but", "in", "on", "at", "to", "for", "of", "with", "by"
])

# Combine with a subset of SpaCy's default stopwords
custom_stopwords = custom_stopwords.union({
    word for word in spacy.lang.en.stop_words.STOP_WORDS 
    if len(word) < 3 or word in ["be", "been", "being", "have", "had", "has", "do", "does", "did", "will", "would", "shall", "should"]
})

# Compile regular expressions for performance
RE_SPECIAL_CHARS = re.compile(r"[^a-zA-Z0-9\s\-'.,?!]")
RE_EXTRA_SPACES = re.compile(r'\s+')

def expand_contractions(text):
    """Expand contractions in the given text using the contractions library."""
    return contractions.fix(text)

def preprocess_texts(texts):
    """
    Preprocess a list of texts by expanding contractions and removing special characters.
    """
    # Expand contractions
    texts = [expand_contractions(text) for text in texts]
    
    # Remove special characters except allowed punctuation
    texts = [RE_SPECIAL_CHARS.sub('', text) for text in texts]
    
    # Remove extra spaces
    texts = [RE_EXTRA_SPACES.sub(' ', text).strip() for text in texts]
    
    return texts

def tokenize_and_lemmatize(texts, nlp, custom_stopwords):
    """
    Tokenize and lemmatize a list of preprocessed texts using SpaCy's nlp.pipe.
    """
    cleaned_texts = []
    for doc in nlp.pipe(texts, batch_size=1000, n_process=cpu_count()-1):
        tokens = [
            token.lemma_ if token.lemma_ != "-PRON-" else token.text.lower()
            for token in doc
            if token.text.lower() not in custom_stopwords and not token.is_punct and not token.is_space
        ]
        cleaned_texts.append(' '.join(tokens))
    return cleaned_texts

def clean_column(df, column_name, new_column_name, nlp, custom_stopwords):
    """
    Clean a specific column in the dataframe and store the result in a new column.
    """
    # Preprocess texts 
    preprocessed_texts = preprocess_texts(df[column_name].astype(str).tolist())
    
    # Tokenize and lemmatize
    cleaned_texts = tokenize_and_lemmatize(preprocessed_texts, nlp, custom_stopwords)
    
    # Assign to new column
    df[new_column_name] = cleaned_texts
    return df

# Apply cleaning to 'Patient' and 'Description' columns
df = clean_column(df, 'Patient', 'patient_clean', nlp, custom_stopwords)
df = clean_column(df, 'Description', 'description_clean', nlp, custom_stopwords)

# remove the description that start with q
df['description_clean'] = df['description_clean'].apply(lambda x: x[2:] if x.startswith('q ') else x)

# Display the cleaned data
print(df[['Patient', 'patient_clean', 'Description', 'description_clean']].head())

3.1b Second stage of text cleaning¶

In [40]:
import re
import pandas as pd
import contractions

def clean_text_second_pass(text):
    # Expand contractions
    text = contractions.fix(text)
    
    # Remove 'Q.' and 'q.' at the beginning of the text
    text = re.sub(r'^[Qq]\.\s*', '', text)
    
    # Convert to lowercase
    text = text.lower()
    
    # Remove special characters except periods, commas, hyphens, and apostrophes
    text = re.sub(r'[^a-z0-9\s.,\'\-]', '', text)
    
    # Replace multiple spaces with a single space
    text = re.sub(r'\s+', ' ', text).strip()
    
    # Preserve common medical abbreviations and units
    text = re.sub(r'\b(hiv)\b', lambda m: m.group(0).upper(), text)
    
    return text

def clean_dataframe_second_pass(df):
    # Apply second pass cleaning to 'description_clean' column
    df['description_clean_2nd_pass'] = df['description_clean'].apply(clean_text_second_pass)
    
    # Apply second pass cleaning to 'patient_clean' column
    df['patient_clean_2nd_pass'] = df['patient_clean'].apply(clean_text_second_pass)
    
    return df


cleaned_df = clean_dataframe_second_pass(df)

# Display the first few rows of the cleaned dataframe
print(cleaned_df[['Description', 'description_clean', 'description_clean_2nd_pass']].head())
print("\n")
print(cleaned_df[['Patient', 'patient_clean', 'patient_clean_2nd_pass']].head())

import re

def clean_text_third_pass(text):
    # Capitalize first letter of sentences
    text = '. '.join(sentence.capitalize() for sentence in text.split('. '))
    
    # Preserve medical terms and units
    medical_terms = ['HIV', 'F', 'kg']
    for term in medical_terms:
        text = re.sub(r'\b' + term.lower() + r'\b', term, text)
    
    # Fix common grammatical issues
    text = re.sub(r'\bbe\b', 'is', text)
    text = re.sub(r'\bbecause\b', 'because', text)
    
    # Remove redundant words
    text = re.sub(r'\s+not\s+sure\b', '', text)
    
    # Fix number formatting
    text = re.sub(r'(\d+)\s*to\s*(\d+)', r'\1-\2', text)
    
    return text.strip()

def clean_dataframe_third_pass(df):
    df['patient_clean_3rd_pass'] = df['patient_clean_2nd_pass'].apply(clean_text_third_pass)
    return df

# Apply third pass cleaning
cleaned_df = clean_dataframe_third_pass(df)

# Display the results
print(cleaned_df[['patient_clean_2nd_pass', 'patient_clean_3rd_pass']].head())

import pandas as pd
import re

def clean_text_final_pass(text):
    # Capitalize first letter of sentences
    text = '. '.join(sentence.capitalize() for sentence in text.split('. '))
    
    # Fix common grammatical issues
    text = re.sub(r'\b(is|be|am|are|was|were)\b', 'is', text, flags=re.IGNORECASE)
    text = re.sub(r'\b(get|gets|getting)\b', 'gets', text, flags=re.IGNORECASE)
    text = re.sub(r'\b(feel|feels|feeling)\b', 'feels', text, flags=re.IGNORECASE)
    
    # Improve readability
    text = re.sub(r'(\d+)\s*(f|kg|min)\b', r'\1 \2', text, flags=re.IGNORECASE)
    text = re.sub(r'\s+', ' ', text).strip()  # Remove extra spaces
    
    # Fix specific phrases
    text = re.sub(r'\bthink\s+(?:is|am|are)\s+go(?:ing)?\s+(?:to)?\s+die\b', 'think I am going to die', text, flags=re.IGNORECASE)
    text = re.sub(r'\bwhat\s+(?:to)?\s*deal\b', 'what to deal with', text, flags=re.IGNORECASE)
    text = re.sub(r'\b(?:not|dont|don\'t)\s+know\b', 'do not know', text, flags=re.IGNORECASE)
    
    # Standardize medical terms
    text = re.sub(r'\bhiv\b', 'HIV', text, flags=re.IGNORECASE)
    
    return text

# Apply the final cleaning function to create a new column
try:
    df['patient_clean_final'] = df['patient_clean_3rd_pass'].apply(clean_text_final_pass)
    print("Final cleaning applied successfully.")
    
    # Display the first few rows of the DataFrame to compare
    print("\nSample results:")
    print(df[['patient_clean_3rd_pass', 'patient_clean_final']].head())
    
    # Print some statistics
    print(f"\nTotal rows processed: {len(df)}")
    print(f"Columns in DataFrame: {df.columns.tolist()}")
    
except Exception as e:
    print(f"An error occurred: {e}")
    print("Please check that your DataFrame and column names are correct.")

1  Hi. You have really done well with the hypothyroidism problem. Your levels are normal with less medications which are very good. As it is genetically induced, it is very difficult to lose weight. My advice to you is, you should focus on maintaining normal levels of TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) and try to remain active, having a positive outlook in life. Or else, it will become very difficult to balance your life with the symptoms of hypothyroidism. Even though your weight has not reduced, be very careful in not putting on weight here afterward. Everyday brisk walking for 1 hour. If you have body pain, alternate with exercises and walking. Avoid all kinds of junk foods, processed, bakery products, rich sweets, fatty foods, sodas, alcohol, and smoking. Avoid partying and binge eating. Follow the food timings properly. Have small frequent meals. In between snacks should be strictly fruits or any kind of low-calorie foods. Have unsalted nuts around five daily. It can give a glow to your dry skin. Everyday water intake should be around 1.5-2 liters. You can use flax seeds. Powder it and mix it in your food. It is a fiber which will give you fullness. Use turmeric, fenugreek seeds, or powder every day. It is a good antioxidant and fenugreek helps in reducing cholesterol levels. Include low-fat milk, curd every day. Egg white, lean chicken, or fish can be taken daily in moderation (anyone). Organ meats need to be avoided. Is your menstrual cycle normal? Please get back if you have any other complaints. Follow up after 15 days.

The HIV test uses a finger prick blood sample, with results given within 20 minutes, and is 99 % accurate at detecting any HIV exposure that may have occurred more than 12 weeks ago. However, it can potentially pick up HIV infection from as little as four weeks ago. There is nothing to worry nothing will happen, and please repeat your test after 12 weeks. If you want accurate results to get, it has done RNA PCR which will give actual results within 10days. Antigen detection like P24 gives best results with in two to four weeks. Probably your suffering from a simple viral upper respiratory infection. After 12 weeks, please consult your doctor he will examine and treat you accordingly.

3.2 Tokenization¶

In this project, tokenization was primarily used for visualizing the patient descriptions being fed into the T5 model. Although the model handles tokenization internally during training, manually tokenizing the data allowed for better insight into the structure of the input, ensuring the data was appropriately prepared for the model.Before tokenizing both features, the dataframe was saved to track the dataset and the processes applied to it. The dataset has now been loaded from this newly saved file

import re
from nltk.corpus import stopwords
import nltk
nltk.download('stopwords')

stop_words = set(stopwords.words('english')) - {'no', 'not'}

def preprocess_for_summarization(text):
    # Tokenize while keeping punctuation
    tokens = re.findall(r'\b[\w\']+\b|[.,!?;]', text.lower())
    # Remove stopwords and very short tokens
    tokens = [token for token in tokens if token not in stop_words and len(token) > 1]
    return tokens

df['processed_tokens'] = df['patient_clean'].apply(preprocess_for_summarization)

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from collections import Counter
from wordcloud import WordCloud
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns



def plot_summary_length_distribution(df):
    df['summary_length'] = df['description_clean'].str.split().str.len()
    
    plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6))
    sns.histplot(data=df, x='summary_length', kde=True, bins=30)
    plt.title('Summary Length Distribution', fontsize=16)
    plt.xlabel('Number of Words', fontsize=12)
    plt.ylabel('Frequency', fontsize=12)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

def get_common_words(df, column='patient_clean', n=20):
    all_words = ' '.join(df[column]).lower().split()
    return Counter(all_words).most_common(n)

def plot_common_words(common_words):
    words, counts = zip(*common_words)
    plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6))
    sns.barplot(x=list(words), y=list(counts))
    plt.title('Most Common Words in Patient Descriptions', fontsize=16)
    plt.xlabel('Words', fontsize=12)
    plt.ylabel('Frequency', fontsize=12)
    plt.xticks(rotation=45, ha='right')
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

def generate_wordcloud(df, column='patient_clean'):
    text = ' '.join(df[column])
    wordcloud = WordCloud(width=800, height=400, background_color='white', 
                          max_words=100, contour_width=3, contour_color='steelblue')
    wordcloud.generate(text)
    
    plt.figure(figsize=(15, 7.5))
    plt.imshow(wordcloud, interpolation='bilinear')
    plt.axis('off')
    plt.title('Word Cloud of Patient Descriptions', fontsize=16)
    plt.tight_layout(pad=0)
    plt.show()

4.Data Preperation¶

After completing the text cleaning and tokenization, we will begin working on summarization. Before training, we have saved all the files so that when we need to run the code again, we don't have to repeat all the processing. This will save our time.For the summarization, we are using the t5-small transformer. Creating a summary and running it locally isn't the end goal. Pushing it one step further is necessary. Therefore, we used a lightweight transformer architecture so that we can use the saved model in production on a free tier version

import torch
from torch.utils.data import Dataset
class SummarizationDataset(Dataset):
    def __init__(self, data, tokenizer, max_input_length=512, max_target_length=150):
        """
        Initializes the dataset with data and tokenizer.

        Args:
            data (list of tuples): List containing (input_text, target_text) pairs.
            tokenizer (transformers.PreTrainedTokenizer): Tokenizer for encoding the text.
            max_input_length (int, optional): Maximum length for input sequences.
            max_target_length (int, optional): Maximum length for target sequences.
        """
        self.data = data
        self.tokenizer = tokenizer
        self.max_input_length = max_input_length
        self.max_target_length = max_target_length

    def __len__(self):
        """
        Returns the total number of samples in the dataset.
        """
        return len(self.data)

    def __getitem__(self, index):
        """
        Retrieves the sample at the specified index.

        Args:
            index (int): Index of the sample to retrieve.

        Returns:
            dict: Dictionary containing input_ids, attention_mask, and labels tensors.
        """
        input_text, target_text = self.data[index]
        
        # Encode the inputs
        input_encoding = self.tokenizer.encode_plus(
            input_text,
            max_length=self.max_input_length,
            padding='max_length',
            truncation=True,
            return_attention_mask=True,
            return_tensors='pt'
        )
        
        # Encode the targets
        target_encoding = self.tokenizer.encode_plus(
            target_text,
            max_length=self.max_target_length,
            padding='max_length',
            truncation=True,
            return_attention_mask=True,
            return_tensors='pt'
        )
        
        return {
            'input_ids': input_encoding['input_ids'].flatten(),
            'attention_mask': input_encoding['attention_mask'].flatten(),
            'labels': target_encoding['input_ids'].flatten()
        }

In [125]:
from torch.utils.tensorboard import SummaryWriter

# Initialize TensorBoard writer
writer = SummaryWriter('runs/t5_training')

# Define Early Stopping parameters
best_val_loss = float('inf')
patience = 5  # Number of epochs to wait for improvement
trigger_times = 0

# Define the number of epochs
epochs = 10

for epoch in range(epochs):
    # ---------------------
    # Training Phase
    # ---------------------
    model.train()
    print(f"\nEpoch {epoch + 1}/{epochs}")
    epoch_loss = 0

    for batch in tqdm(train_loader, desc="Training"):
        # Move batch to the device
        input_ids = batch['input_ids'].to(device)
        attention_mask = batch['attention_mask'].to(device)
        labels = batch['labels'].to(device)

        # Clear gradients
        optimizer.zero_grad()

        # Forward pass
        outputs = model(input_ids=input_ids, attention_mask=attention_mask, labels=labels)
        loss = outputs.loss
        epoch_loss += loss.item()

        # Backward pass
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

    # Calculate average training loss for the epoch
    avg_epoch_loss = epoch_loss / len(train_loader)
    print(f"Average Training Loss: {avg_epoch_loss:.4f}")

    # Log training loss to TensorBoard
    writer.add_scalar('Loss/Train', avg_epoch_loss, epoch)

    # ---------------------
    # Validation Phase
    # ---------------------
    model.eval()
    val_loss = 0

    with torch.no_grad():
        for batch in tqdm(val_loader, desc="Validation"):
            input_ids = batch['input_ids'].to(device)
            attention_mask = batch['attention_mask'].to(device)
            labels = batch['labels'].to(device)

            # Forward pass
            outputs = model(input_ids=input_ids, attention_mask=attention_mask, labels=labels)
            loss = outputs.loss
            val_loss += loss.item()

    # Calculate average validation loss for the epoch
    avg_val_loss = val_loss / len(val_loader)
    print(f"Average Validation Loss: {avg_val_loss:.4f}")

    # Log validation loss to TensorBoard
    writer.add_scalar('Loss/Validation', avg_val_loss, epoch)

    # ---------------------
    # Early Stopping Check
    # ---------------------
    if avg_val_loss < best_val_loss:
        best_val_loss = avg_val_loss
        trigger_times = 0
        # Save the best model
        model.save_pretrained("best_t5_model")
        tokenizer.save_pretrained("best_t5_model")
        print("Validation loss improved. Model saved.")
    else:
        trigger_times += 1
        print(f"EarlyStopping counter: {trigger_times} out of {patience}")
        if trigger_times >= patience:
            print("Early stopping triggered!")
            break

# Close TensorBoard writer
writer.close()

6.Model Evaluation¶

For evaluating the performance of our summarization model, we used the ROUGE metric, specifically ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L. These metrics help us measure the overlap between the generated summaries and the reference summaries, capturing both unigram/bigram accuracy and overall fluency

from tqdm import tqdm
import logging

# Set up logging to a file to avoid overloading Jupyter output
logging.basicConfig(filename='summary_generation.log', level=logging.INFO)

def generate_summaries(model, tokenizer, dataloader, device, max_length=150, min_length=40):
    """
    Generates summaries for the given dataset.

    Args:
        model (transformers.PreTrainedModel): The trained model.
        tokenizer (transformers.PreTrainedTokenizer): The tokenizer.
        dataloader (DataLoader): DataLoader for the dataset.
        device (torch.device): Device to run the model on.
        max_length (int, optional): Maximum length of the generated summary.
        min_length (int, optional): Minimum length of the generated summary.

    Returns:
        list: Generated summaries.
        list: Reference summaries.
    """
    best_model.eval()
    summaries = []
    references = []

    with torch.no_grad():
        for i, batch in enumerate(tqdm(dataloader, desc="Generating Summaries", mininterval=10)):  # Reduce tqdm verbosity
            input_ids = batch['input_ids'].to(device)
            attention_mask = batch['attention_mask'].to(device)

            # Generate summaries
            generated_ids = model.generate(
                input_ids=input_ids,
                attention_mask=attention_mask,
                max_length=max_length,
                min_length=min_length,
                num_beams=4,
                early_stopping=True
            )

            # Decode summaries
            decoded_summaries = tokenizer.batch_decode(generated_ids, skip_special_tokens=True)
            summaries.extend(decoded_summaries)

            # Decode references without modifying labels
            labels = batch['labels']
            decoded_references = tokenizer.batch_decode(labels, skip_special_tokens=True)
            references.extend(decoded_references)

            # Log progress to avoid overwhelming Jupyter output
            logging.info(f"Batch {i+1}/{len(dataloader)} processed.")

    return summaries, references

# Generate summaries and references on the test set
test_summaries, test_references = generate_summaries(best_model, best_tokenizer, test_loader, device)

from rouge_score import rouge_scorer
import numpy as np

def compute_rouge(predictions, references):
    """
    Computes average ROUGE scores between predictions and references.

    Args:
        predictions (list): Generated summaries.
        references (list): Reference summaries.

    Returns:
        dict: Average ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L scores.
    """
    scorer = rouge_scorer.RougeScorer(['rouge1', 'rouge2', 'rougeL'], use_stemmer=True)
    scores = {'rouge1': [], 'rouge2': [], 'rougeL': []}
    
    for pred, ref in zip(predictions, references):
        score = scorer.score(ref, pred)
        scores['rouge1'].append(score['rouge1'].fmeasure)
        scores['rouge2'].append(score['rouge2'].fmeasure)
        scores['rougeL'].append(score['rougeL'].fmeasure)
    
    # Calculate average scores
    avg_scores = {metric: np.mean(values) for metric, values in scores.items()}
    return avg_scores

# Compute ROUGE scores
test_rouge_scores = compute_rouge(test_summaries, test_references)

# Display the scores
print("\nTest ROUGE Scores:")
for metric, score in test_rouge_scores.items():
    print(f"{metric}: {score:.4f}")

def display_samples(inputs, summaries, references, num_examples=3):
    """
    Displays sample inputs, reference summaries, and generated summaries.

    Args:
        inputs (list): List of input texts.
        summaries (list): List of generated summaries.
        references (list): List of reference summaries.

    """
    for i in range(num_examples):
        print(f"--- Example {i+1} ---")
        print(f"Input: {inputs[i]}")
        print(f"Reference Summary: {references[i]}")
        print(f"Model Summary: {summaries[i]}\n")

# Extract test inputs for display
def get_test_inputs(dataloader, num_examples=3):
    """
    Extracts a limited number of input texts from the dataloader for display.

    Args:
        dataloader (DataLoader): DataLoader for the dataset.
        num_examples (int): Number of examples to retrieve.

    Returns:
        list: Decoded input texts.
    """
    inputs = []
    for batch in dataloader:
        input_ids = batch['input_ids']
        input_texts = best_tokenizer.batch_decode(input_ids, skip_special_tokens=True)
        inputs.extend(input_texts)
        if len(inputs) >= num_examples:
            break
    return inputs[:num_examples]

Based on the summaries generated from the test set, we observed frequent word repetition during the model’s summarization. To address this issue, we plan to fine-tune the model and adjust the parameters to improve performance. Due to the repetition and the model’s difficulty in properly capturing context, the ROUGE scores are currently relatively low.

7.Fine Tuning¶

from transformers import T5Tokenizer, T5ForConditionalGeneration
import torch

model_path = "best_t5_model"
best_model = T5ForConditionalGeneration.from_pretrained(model_path).to(device)
best_tokenizer = T5Tokenizer.from_pretrained(model_path)
best_model.eval()  

# Define a single sentence input text
single_input = "summarize: The patient is experiencing mild headaches and occasional dizziness."


# Tokenize the input
input_encoding = best_tokenizer.encode_plus(
    single_input,
    max_length=512,
    padding='max_length',
    truncation=True,
    return_attention_mask=True,
    return_tensors='pt'
)

attention_mask = input_encoding['attention_mask'].to(device)

        attention_mask=attention_mask,
        max_length=50,

        repetition_penalty=2.0,  # Penalize repetition
        length_penalty=1.5,      # Encourage conciseness
        early_stopping=True
    )
    summary = best_tokenizer.decode(summary_ids[0], skip_special_tokens=True)
    print(f"Generated Summary: {summary}")
except Exception as e:

After fine-tuning, we set up the model with specific rules for creating text. We tell it that each piece of text should be between 10 and 50 words long. We also make sure it doesn't repeat itself too much. To keep things interesting, we let the model choose from the 50 most likely words each time, but it can only pick from the top 95% of choices to avoid weird results. Lastly, we set the "temperature" to 1.0, which means the model can be quite creative in its word choices. This balance of rules helps the model generate text that's varied and suitable for our needs and solve the previous repitation problem.

After the poor performance in the initial testing phase, we will evaluate the test set using our previous model with the generate method, applying techniques like top-k sampling, nucleus sampling, and a repetition penalty to see how much the performance has improved

from tqdm import tqdm
import logging

# Set up logging to a file to avoid overloading Jupyter output
logging.basicConfig(filename='summary_generation.log', level=logging.INFO)

def generate_summaries(model, tokenizer, dataloader, device, max_length=50, min_length=10):
    """
    Generates summaries for the given dataset using sampling.

    Args:
        model (transformers.PreTrainedModel): The trained model.
        tokenizer (transformers.PreTrainedTokenizer): The tokenizer.
        dataloader (DataLoader): DataLoader for the dataset.
        device (torch.device): Device to run the model on.
        max_length (int, optional): Maximum length of the generated summary.
        min_length (int, optional): Minimum length of the generated summary.

    Returns:
        list: Generated summaries.
        list: Reference summaries.
    """
    model.eval()
    summaries = []
    references = []

    with torch.no_grad():
        for i, batch in enumerate(tqdm(dataloader, desc="Generating Summaries", mininterval=10)):  # Reduce tqdm verbosity
            input_ids = batch['input_ids'].to(device)
            attention_mask = batch['attention_mask'].to(device)

            # Generate summaries with sampling parameters for variability
            generated_ids = model.generate(
                input_ids=input_ids,
                attention_mask=attention_mask,
                max_length=max_length,
                min_length=min_length,
                repetition_penalty=2.0,
                do_sample=True,          # Enable sampling for variability
                top_k=50,                # Top-k sampling for diversity
                top_p=0.95,              # Nucleus sampling for natural phrasing
                temperature=1.0          # Control randomness in generation
            )

            # Decode summaries and reference summaries
            decoded_summaries = tokenizer.batch_decode(generated_ids, skip_special_tokens=True)
            summaries.extend(decoded_summaries)

            # Decode reference summaries
            labels = batch['labels']
            decoded_references = tokenizer.batch_decode(labels, skip_special_tokens=True)
            references.extend(decoded_references)

            # Log progress to avoid overwhelming Jupyter output
            logging.info(f"Batch {i+1}/{len(dataloader)} processed.")

    return summaries, references

# Generate summaries and references on the test set with updated parameters
test_summaries, test_references = generate_summaries(best_model, best_tokenizer, test_loader, device)

After applying fine-tuning to my model, the generated summaries have improved compared to the previous results. The ROUGE score has increased, and repetition has been eliminated. The model's summaries are now more closely aligned with the reference summaries. However, there is still room for improvement. One notable observation is that the target column (descriptions) often starts sentences with 'why,' 'what,' or 'where.' Our fine-tuned T5 model has learned this pattern, which is reflected in the summaries it generates

8.Conclusion¶

The model is now able to capture the key points from the summaries, which is important for us. Based on these key points, we can further refine our chatbot. Concise summaries will help us understand what our patients are looking for, and we can design prompts accordingly to ensure the chatbot provides the best possible output. One key lesson we learned is that fine-tuning is a powerful tool. There is a significant difference between the model with and without fine-tuning. The repetitive summaries we received earlier, before fine-tuning, would have caused a mismatch when calling our API. For production purposes, we used the T5-small transformer, allowing for real-time decisions from our chatbot efficiently
